chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muskhan, from Muhammad ibn Bashir, from al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I have made it a vow upon myself for the sake of Allah that I will not accept any kinship gift from my paternal uncles' sons, nor will I take out my goods in the market of Mina during those days.' He said, then he said, 'If you made that as an expression of gratitude, then fulfill it; and if you merely said that out of anger, then there is no obligation upon you.'

key_terms.سُوقِ مِنًى: The market of Mina, a location associated with Hajj rituals
key_terms.صِلَة: Kinship ties or gifts given to maintain family relations
key_terms.نُذُور: Vows or pledges made to God

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a vow made out of anger and one made out of gratitude in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between vows made as genuine acts of gratitude (*shukr*) and those made impulsively out of anger (*ghadab*). He clarifies that while a vow of gratitude is binding and must be fulfilled, a vow born of emotional outburst carries no obligation, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that intent (*niyyah*) determines the validity of the vow. This distinction highlights the importance of emotional state in personal vows, ensuring that temporary anger does not lead to unnecessary religious burdens.
